newsitem.title: PERU: Angry exchanges on month anniversary of Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Angry exchanges on month anniversary of Peru siege.

text.p: An angry exchange of accusations of manipulation and bad faith left Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages seething on Friday on the month's anniversary of their standoff.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo rejected on Thursday a rebel proposal that the Guatemalan government take part in talks to end the siege and said he had cut off Red Cross and family visits to jailed members of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini replied in a megaphone tirade from the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence that the government was creating obstacles to solving the crisis.
He ruled out more hostage releases anytime soon.
Police then told about 16 photographers and TV cameramen camped out on a roof opposite the residence -- the closest media vantage point -- that they would have to get down.

"You are all coming down tonight," police Col. Fernando Zapata said. Local media, who have had representatives on the roof since the siege began Dec. 17, obeyed but international reporters did not immediately move and were not forced.

At the same time the MRTA sent a message to journalists on their "Rebel Voice" Internet page: "There does not exist a fear on our part of speaking with journalists or to journalists observing what is happening inside the residence."

The message signed by the rebels' international spokesman Isaac Velazco also called for the media to be allowed into Peruvian prisons to see the conditions of some 400 jailed MRTA members. The prisoners' release is the rebels' main demand.

Palermo told a news conference the government considered that trying to bring Guatemala into the talks was an effort by the rebels to suggest a similarity between the situation in Peru and the recently ended civil war in the Central American country where leftist guerrillas laid down arms in December after more than 30 years of fighting.
"With this suggestion the aim is to establish an analogy with a completely different reality," Palermo said.
According to released hostages Cerpa told them the MRTA was willing to lay down its arms and become a political party.

The Peruvian government says the hostage takers are "terrorists" with no support among the population. It claims it is a false parallel to compare Central American guerrilla conflicts of the 1980s and early 1990s and its fight against the MRTA and the larger Maoist Shining Path movement.
Cerpa balked at the label "terrorists," saying: "With these arguments it is difficult to reach an accord."
The rebels suggested on Wednesday that Guatemala and an unnamed European country join a "guarantor commission" proposed by the government to oversee talks to end the crisis.
Both sides agreed to the participation of representatives from the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Vatican.

Cerpa attempted to reply to Palermo with a statement read to reporters by walkie-talkie, but was barely intelligible due to heavy distortion. Police had earlier broken into the frequency used by the rebels and reporters at the scene suspected the transmission was being jammed by authorities.

Cerpa then used a megaphone to shout a statement. He asked for the visits by the Red Cross and relatives of MRTA prisoners in government jails to be resumed, saying a sign of "good will" was needed from the government of President Alberto Fujimori.
Palermo said the visits to MRTA prisoners were being suspended "in order to avoid disturbing the process of talks" but did not explain how such visits had been doing so.

Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter -- an experienced negotiator in trouble spots around the world -- said on a trip in neighbouring Chile he would be "delighted" to act as a mediator in the crisis if both sides asked.
Fujimori has flatly ruled out releasing MRTA prisoners but says he would consider letting the rebels leave Peru if they laid down their arms and freed all their hostages.
